To hoodwink someone means to deliberately trick or deceive them, usually by feeding them false information or creating a false impression — so that they believe something that is not true, and you (or someone else) benefit from their belief.

It is always an intentional act. Nobody hoodwinks someone by accident. There is always a deceiver who plans the trick and a victim who falls for it.
What Makes It Different From Just "Lying"

A simple lie is one false statement. Hoodwinking is bigger than that. It carries the sense of carefully constructing a false picture of reality in someone's mind, so completely that the victim has no idea they are being deceived. The person being hoodwinked genuinely and fully believes the false thing. They walk away feeling confident and informed — not knowing they have been played.

Think of it this way: if someone tells you "the shop is closed today" and it isn't, they lied to you. But if a fraudster builds a fake website, creates fake customer reviews, sends you fake receipts, and convinces you to invest your savings into a company that doesn't exist — that is hoodwinking. The deception is crafted, layered, and sustained.
The Relationship Between Deceiver and Victim

Hoodwinking almost always involves an imbalance of knowledge and trust:

  • The deceiver knows the full truth and deliberately hides it.
  • The victim trusts the deceiver (or at least has no reason to distrust them) and is therefore vulnerable.

This is why hoodwinking feels especially cruel when discovered. The victim wasn't just wrong — they were kept wrong by someone who knew better and used that knowledge against them.

The victim is typically portrayed as innocent, naive, or simply trusting — not stupid. Smart, careful people get hoodwinked too, because the deception is designed to be believable.
How It Feels to Be Hoodwinked

When someone discovers they have been hoodwinked, they usually feel:

  • Betrayed — because trust was abused
  • Embarrassed — because they believed something false
  • Angry — because the deception was deliberate

This emotional weight is baked into the word. Saying "I was hoodwinked" communicates not just that you were deceived, but that you feel the sting of that betrayal.

Here are examples that show the word used naturally:

  • "The company hoodwinked thousands of customers into paying for a service that never existed."
  • "Don't let smooth talkers hoodwink you — always read the fine print."
  • "She only realised she had been hoodwinked when the money never arrived."
  • "He hoodwinked the entire committee by presenting fake research data."
  • "Voters felt completely hoodwinked after the politician broke every promise he made."

Notice that the passive form ("was hoodwinked / had been hoodwinked") is very common, because it emphasises the victim's perspective — they are on the receiving end of the deception.

Hoodwinking happens in all kinds of situations:

  • Financial fraud — investors tricked into fake schemes
  • Politics — citizens misled by false promises
  • Sales — buyers deceived about a product's quality
  • Personal relationships — someone lied to by a partner or friend
  • Institutional deception — authorities or governments misled by falsified information

The word fits almost any situation where deliberate deception leads someone to believe a false reality.

"Hoodwink" sits comfortably between informal and semi-formal. It appears in:

  • Everyday conversation ("I can't believe he hoodwinked me!")
  • News articles and journalism ("The public was hoodwinked by misleading statistics.")
  • Fiction and storytelling

It has a slightly colourful, vivid feel compared to more neutral words like "deceive" or "mislead." It is never rude or offensive — perfectly appropriate in professional and academic writing, while still feeling natural in everyday speech.
How It Compares to Similar Words

WordHow it differs from "hoodwink"
DeceiveMore neutral and formal; covers any form of deception
MisleadOften unintentional, or involves giving incomplete information
ConMore casual; often implies a quick scam
DupeEmphasises the victim's gullibility more than the deceiver's cleverness
FoolGeneral; doesn't always imply sustained or planned deception
BamboozleVery similar to hoodwink but slightly more playful in tone

Hoodwink specifically emphasises that the deception was deliberate, calculated, and successful — the victim fully believed the false reality that was created for them.

To hoodwink someone = to deliberately and successfully trick them into believing something false, usually for your own gain, in a way that leaves them completely unaware they have been deceived.

The word always implies intent, cleverness on the part of the deceiver, and the victim's genuine (though false) belief. It is a word that carries moral weight — to call someone a hoodwinker is to call them dishonest and manipulative.
